Watch why the deal is being viewed as a capitulation » . Swat Valley was once one of Pakistan's biggest tourist destinations. It is situated near the Afghanistan border and about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from Pakistan's capital, Islamabad. The militants want to require veils for women and beards for men and to ban music and television. The fighting has displaced nearly half of Swat's population, officials said. Keywords: WASHINGTON, CNN, Pakistan

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Pakistan is optimistic about the Obama administration's commitment to its region and is prepared to work with the United States in its efforts to root out extremism within its borders, Pakistan's foreign minister said.

Following a meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Pakistani Foreign Minister Makhdoom Shah Mehmood Qureshi pointed to a "convergence of interests" between Washington and Islamabad and a mutual "willingness to work together."

"I see a great deal of hope in the new administration and the new leadership, and Pakistan is willing to work with the American administration to fight extremism and terrorism," he said Tuesday. "We are determined to defeat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations."

Qureshi is in Washington to take part in a strategic review of U.S. policy aimed at stabilizing Afghanistan and neighboring Pakistan. The effort is being led by South Asian security expert Bruce Reidel and Ambassador Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special envoy.

Afghan Foreign Minister Rangin D. Spanta is also heading a delegation from his country to participate in the review. Both he and Qureshi are scheduled to meet with Clinton and Holbrooke this week.

U.S. President Barack Obama and Clinton appointed Holbrooke as special representative for the two nations—a clear signal of how deeply the new administration regards Afghanistan and Pakistan as intertwined in any solution to the war in Afghanistan and the terrorist threat along their shared border.

"We are consulting very closely with the government of Pakistan on our strategic review of our way forward, and I am most grateful for the minister's advice and counsel," Clinton said after her meeting with Qureshi.

Last week, Obama announced that he is deploying an additional 17,000 troops to Afghanistan to confront a strengthening insurgency, which he has described as the "central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism." The troops will be sent to southern Afghanistan, a region that borders Pakistan and serves as a haven for Taliban insurgents. Pakistani officials have voiced concern that the deployment could push the Taliban across the border into Pakistan, further destabilizing their country.

The Obama administration is undertaking several reviews of U.S. policy in Afghanistan, including one led by Gen. David Petraeus, the commander in the region. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has stated that the original mission in Afghanistan was "too broad" and must become more "realistic and focused" if the United States is to succeed.

Pakistan is likewise engaged in its own campaign against Taliban militants in its Northwest Frontier Province. The militants, who effectively control the country's Swat Valley, extended a cease-fire Tuesday as part of an agreement with the government—a deal that the U.S. and NATO warn risks granting extremists a safe haven near the Afghan border. Watch why the deal is being viewed as a capitulation »

The Swat Valley was once among Pakistan's premier tourist destinations. Situated near the Afghanistan border, it lies about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from Pakistan's capital, Islamabad. In recent months, militants have unleashed a wave of violence that has claimed hundreds of lives across the province. The militants seek to require veils for women and beards for men, and to ban music and television. The fighting has displaced nearly half of Swat's population, officials said.

Although the central government has long exerted little control over the area, it launched an intense military offensive in late July to drive out the militants. In retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly bombings, beheadings, and kidnappings, vowing that the attacks would continue until the troops withdrew.

On Tuesday, the Taliban announced that it was indefinitely extending a cease-fire its leaders had declared eight days earlier, following the signing of a controversial deal with the government to impose Islamic law, or Sharia, in the region. The Pakistani government's decision to negotiate with the Taliban has drawn international criticism.

Holbrooke has said the Obama administration was "troubled and confused" by the truce in Swat. Both Holbrooke and NATO officials have expressed concern that such an accord could effectively cede control of the Swat Valley to extremists.

"We are consulting very closely with the government of Pakistan on our strategic review of our way forward and I'm very grateful for the minister's advice and counsel," Clinton remarked following her talks with Qureshi.

The previous week, Obama declared that an additional 17,000 soldiers would be deployed to Afghanistan to confront a growing insurgency, which he has labeled the "central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism." These forces are headed to southern Afghanistan, a region bordering Pakistan that serves as a sanctuary for Taliban fighters.

Officials in Pakistan have voiced worry that this deployment could drive Taliban militants across the border into their own nation, adding to its instability.

The Obama administration is carrying out multiple evaluations of American strategy in Afghanistan, among them one directed by Gen. David Petraeus, who commands forces in the area. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has commented that the initial objectives in Afghanistan were "too broad" and require a more "realistic and focused" approach if the United States is to prevail.

Meanwhile, Pakistan is waging its own campaign against Taliban fighters in its Northwest Frontier Province. These militants, who essentially dominate the Swat Valley, prolonged a cease-fire on Tuesday under an arrangement with the government—a deal that the U.S. and NATO caution could hand extremists a refuge close to the Afghan border.

The Swat Valley was formerly among Pakistan's premier tourist attractions. Located near the Afghan boundary, it lies roughly 186 miles (300 kilometers) from Islamabad, the Pakistani capital. Over recent months, militants have launched a surge of violence that has taken hundreds of lives throughout the province. They seek to mandate veils for women and beards for men while prohibiting both music and television.

According to officials, the conflict has forced nearly half of Swat's residents from their homes. Although the central government has historically held minimal authority in the region, it began a fierce military campaign in late July to drive out the militants. In response to the troop presence, the Taliban conducted numerous lethal bombings, beheadings, and abductions, vowing that such assaults would persist until the soldiers withdrew.

On Tuesday, the Taliban announced it was extending indefinitely a cease-fire that its leaders had proclaimed eight days earlier, following a contentious agreement with the government to enforce Islamic law, or Sharia, across the region. The Pakistani government's move to enter negotiations has drawn condemnation from the international community.

Holbrooke has said the Obama administration felt "troubled and confused" over the Swat truce. Both Holbrooke and NATO representatives have raised concerns that such a pact might effectively surrender control of the Swat Valley to extremists.

# US-Pakistan Relations Face New Challenges Amid Regional Shifts

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Relations between the United States and Pakistan continue to evolve as both nations navigate a complex web of security concerns, economic partnerships, and regional dynamics in South Asia.

Officials in Washington have long viewed Pakistan as a critical player in regional stability, particularly given its geographic position bordering Afghanistan, India, China, and Iran. The relationship, however, has experienced significant ups and downs over the decades, shaped by shared interests as well as periods of deep mistrust.

## A Complicated Partnership

For years, Pakistan has served as an important, if sometimes uneasy, partner in American counterterrorism efforts. Cooperation intensified following the events of 2001, though tensions occasionally surfaced over questions of security operations and cross-border activities.

In recent years, economic considerations have taken center stage. Pakistan has sought to strengthen ties with multiple global powers, including deepening its relationship with China through infrastructure investments, while maintaining diplomatic channels with Washington.

## Economic and Diplomatic Dimensions

Analysts note that Islamabad's ongoing economic challenges, including debt pressures and inflation, have added urgency to its diplomatic outreach. The United States remains one of Pakistan's largest trading partners and export markets, giving both sides incentive to maintain a working relationship.

"The relationship reflects a balance of strategic interests," one regional expert observed, emphasizing that pragmatism often guides decisions on both sides.

## Looking Ahead

As Washington recalibrates its priorities in the Indo-Pacific region, the future of US-Pakistan relations will likely depend on cooperation across counterterrorism, trade, and broader regional stability. Both nations appear committed to dialogue, even as underlying differences persist.

---

# Pakistani Foreign Minister Meets Clinton to Discuss Counterterrorism Cooperation

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Pakistan's foreign minister met with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Wednesday for high-level talks focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation in the fight against extremism and reviewing American strategy in the region.

The meeting comes at a critical juncture as the Obama administration continues its strategic review of policy toward Afghanistan and Pakistan, two nations viewed as central to U.S. efforts to combat terrorism and regional instability.

## Building a Partnership

Speaking after the meeting, both officials emphasized the importance of the U.S.-Pakistan relationship in addressing shared security concerns.

"The United States values its partnership with Pakistan," Clinton said. "We recognize that the challenges we face require close cooperation, mutual respect, and a shared commitment to peace and stability in the region."

The Pakistani foreign minister underscored his country's sacrifices in the fight against militancy, noting that Pakistan has suffered significant casualties among both its security forces and civilian population.

"Pakistan is committed to combating extremism in all its forms," the foreign minister said. "But we must approach this challenge as genuine partners, with an understanding of the complex realities on the ground."

## Strategic Review in Focus

The discussions took place against the backdrop of Washington's comprehensive review of its Afghanistan-Pakistan strategy. U.S. officials have increasingly emphasized that success in Afghanistan is closely linked to stability in Pakistan, particularly in the border regions where militant groups are believed to operate.

Key topics reportedly included:

- **Counterterrorism cooperation** and intelligence sharing
- **Economic assistance** and development aid to Pakistan
- **Border security** along the Afghanistan-Pakistan frontier
- **Regional stability** and diplomatic coordination

## Challenges Ahead

Analysts note that the relationship, while strategically vital, has faced periodic tensions over issues ranging from drone strikes to concerns about militant safe havens.

Both sides expressed optimism that continued dialogue would help address areas of disagreement while advancing shared goals.

"We don't expect to agree on everything," a senior State Department official said on condition of anonymity. "But the depth of our engagement reflects how seriously both governments take this partnership."

The meeting is expected to be followed by additional high-level exchanges as the two nations work to align their approaches to regional security.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Obama Administration Undertakes Comprehensive Review of Afghanistan-Pakistan Strategy

## White House Signals Major Shift in Regional Approach

WASHINGTON — The Obama administration is conducting an extensive review of its policy toward Afghanistan and Pakistan, signaling a significant recalibration of American strategy in a region that officials increasingly describe as the central front in the fight against terrorism.

The review reflects growing concern within the administration that the situation in Afghanistan has deteriorated substantially, while instability in neighboring Pakistan poses an equally pressing challenge to regional and international security.

## Troop Increase Ordered

In one of his most consequential early decisions, President Obama has authorized the deployment of additional U.S. forces to Afghanistan. The troop increase—numbering roughly 17,000 additional personnel—is intended to address deteriorating security conditions, particularly in the country's volatile southern provinces where Taliban activity has intensified.

Administration officials have framed the deployment as a necessary stabilizing measure ahead of Afghan elections, while emphasizing that a military solution alone will not suffice. The buildup underscores the administration's assessment that additional resources are urgently needed to reverse recent setbacks on the ground.

## Key Figures: Holbrooke and Petraeus

Two prominent figures have emerged as central to the administration's regional strategy.

**Richard Holbrooke**, the veteran diplomat appointed as Special Representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, has taken a leading role in coordinating civilian and diplomatic efforts across both countries. Known for his forceful negotiating style and his earlier work brokering peace in the Balkans, Holbrooke has undertaken extensive travel throughout the region to assess conditions and consult with local leaders. His appointment reflects the administration's emphasis on treating Afghanistan and Pakistan as an interconnected strategic challenge rather than separate theaters.

**General David Petraeus**, commander of U.S. Central Command, oversees military operations across the broader region. Having earned considerable credit for the strategy credited with reducing violence in Iraq, Petraeus brings his counterinsurgency expertise to the Afghan theater. His involvement in shaping military strategy has been closely watched as the administration weighs how best to apply lessons from Iraq to the distinct challenges posed by Afghanistan's terrain, tribal dynamics, and porous border with Pakistan.

## Controversy Over Swat Valley Cease-Fire

The policy review has been complicated by developments in Pakistan, where the government's decision to reach a cease-fire agreement in the Swat Valley has generated significant controversy.

Under the arrangement, Pakistani authorities agreed to permit the implementation of Islamic law in the region in exchange for a cessation of hostilities with militants who had gained effective control over much of the area. The deal has drawn sharp criticism from observers who view it as a concession to extremists and a potential template that could embolden militant groups elsewhere.

U.S. officials have expressed unease over the agreement, viewing it as a troubling sign of the Pakistani government's willingness—or ability—to confront militancy within its own borders. Critics warn that ceding territory and accepting militant demands could provide safe haven for groups operating against both Afghan and coalition forces, undermining broader stabilization efforts.

Defenders of the arrangement within Pakistan have argued that it represents a pragmatic response to a difficult situation and reflects local demands for a functioning justice system, rather than an outright capitulation.

## Broader Strategic Implications

The confluence of these developments—the troop increase, the elevation of Holbrooke and Petraeus, and the Swat Valley controversy—illustrates the complexity confronting the Obama administration as it seeks to craft a coherent regional strategy.

Administration officials have stressed that success will require an integrated approach combining military, diplomatic, and economic tools, along with sustained cooperation from the Pakistani government. The ongoing review is expected to produce a set of clearer strategic objectives and benchmarks intended to guide American policy in the months ahead.

As the administration finalizes its approach, questions remain about the sustainability of the military commitment, the reliability of Pakistan as a partner, and the prospects for meaningful progress in a region that has long frustrated the ambitions of outside powers.

---

*This report reflects developments during the early period of the Obama administration's policy review on Afghanistan and Pakistan.*

# U.S. Voices Concern Over Swat Valley Truce as Pakistani Foreign Minister Visits Washington

**WASHINGTON** — Pakistani Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi held talks with senior U.S. officials this week amid growing international unease over a peace agreement between Pakistan's government and Taliban militants in the strategically important Swat Valley.

The truce, which permits the implementation of Islamic sharia law in the Malakand region in exchange for a cessation of hostilities, has drawn sharp criticism from Washington and other Western capitals concerned that the deal could embolden extremists and cede territory to Taliban influence.

## Balancing Act

Qureshi sought to reassure American officials that the agreement did not represent a capitulation to militant forces. Speaking to reporters, the foreign minister characterized the arrangement as a response to local demands for a swifter justice system rather than an endorsement of Taliban ideology.

"This is not a surrender," Qureshi emphasized during his visit. "This is an effort to isolate the militants from the local population and to restore peace through a mechanism the people of the region have long sought."

The foreign minister argued that Pakistan's approach reflected the complex realities on the ground, where military operations alone had failed to bring lasting stability to the region located roughly 100 miles from the capital, Islamabad.

## American Skepticism

U.S. officials, however, expressed reservations about whether such agreements could hold. The Obama administration, then conducting a comprehensive review of its strategy in Afghanistan and Pakistan, worried that negotiated settlements might provide militants with sanctuary and space to regroup.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and other administration figures had previously voiced concern that concessions to extremist elements could undermine broader efforts to combat terrorism in the region. The Swat truce raised particular alarm given the valley's proximity to major population centers and its history as a former tourist destination now under militant pressure.

Critics pointed to previous peace deals in Pakistan's tribal areas that had collapsed, arguing that such arrangements historically allowed militants to consolidate power rather than lay down their arms.

## Strategic Stakes

The talks unfolded against the backdrop of a critical partnership. The United States viewed Pakistan's cooperation as essential to stabilizing neighboring Afghanistan, where American and NATO forces confronted a resurgent Taliban insurgency.

At the same time, Washington was weighing significant increases in both military and civilian assistance to Pakistan, with lawmakers debating aid packages intended to strengthen the country's democratic institutions and counterterrorism capabilities.

Qureshi's visit underscored the delicate diplomacy required to align the priorities of the two nations. Pakistani officials sought greater economic support and recognition of their domestic challenges, while American counterparts pressed for demonstrable action against militant networks operating within Pakistan's borders.

## Looking Ahead

The foreign minister's discussions were expected to feed into ongoing consultations ahead of anticipated trilateral meetings involving the United States, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. Both sides publicly affirmed their commitment to the partnership, even as differences over tactics remained evident.

As Qureshi concluded his Washington engagements, the fate of the Swat Valley agreement remained uncertain, symbolizing the broader challenges confronting a relationship deemed vital to regional security yet complicated by divergent perspectives on how best to confront a shared threat.

---

*This story reflects the diplomatic climate of early 2009, a period marked by intensive review of U.S. policy toward South Asia and heightened concern over stability in the region.*

# Uneasy Peace: The Swat Valley Sharia Agreement and America's Counterterrorism Dilemma

## A Fragile Bargain in Pakistan's Restive Northwest

In the mountainous reaches of Pakistan's Northwest Frontier Province, a controversial peace agreement has thrown into sharp relief the profound challenges facing both Islamabad and Washington in their struggle against militant extremism. The deal, which effectively permits the implementation of Sharia law across the Malakand Division—including the once-idyllic Swat Valley—represents either a pragmatic path to peace or a dangerous capitulation to militancy, depending on whom one asks.

The Swat Valley, historically a tourist destination often described as the "Switzerland of Pakistan," has in recent years descended into a battleground between government forces and militants aligned with the Tehreek-e-Nafaz-e-Shariat-e-Mohammadi (TNSM) and the broader Pakistani Taliban movement. Years of fighting have displaced hundreds of thousands, shuttered girls' schools, and eroded state authority across the region.

## The Terms of the Agreement

Under the arrangement, provincial authorities agreed to establish Islamic courts and legal procedures in exchange for a cessation of hostilities from militant factions. Proponents within the provincial government, led by the Awami National Party, have characterized the deal as a response to longstanding local demands for swift justice—the region's residents have historically complained about the glacial pace and corruption of Pakistan's conventional court system.

The government's calculus rested on a distinction its officials sought to draw between legitimate demands for Islamic jurisprudence, which they argued had deep roots in the area, and the violent tactics of the militants. By addressing the former, authorities hoped to isolate and delegitimize the latter.

## Skepticism and Alarm

Critics, however, viewed the agreement with deep unease. Human rights advocates warned that the deal represented a surrender of state sovereignty to armed extremists who had demonstrated little inclination toward genuine reconciliation. Previous cease-fires and accords in the region had repeatedly collapsed, often after militants used the pause to consolidate their positions and rearm.

The imagery emerging from Swat—including the flogging of a young woman that circulated widely and provoked national outrage—underscored fears that the peace would come at the expense of civil liberties, particularly for women and religious minorities. Girls' education, a frequent target of militant ire, remained precariously endangered.

## The Washington Perspective

For American policymakers, the Swat agreement crystallized the fundamental tension at the heart of counterterrorism strategy in the region. U.S. officials expressed public concern that any deal ceding territory or authority to militants risked creating sanctuaries from which extremists could operate with impunity—the very conditions that had allowed al-Qaeda and affiliated groups to flourish in the tribal belt.

The proximity of Swat to major population centers, and its relative distance from the traditional Federally Administered Tribal Areas, made the agreement particularly worrisome. If militancy could take root in a settled district like Swat, the argument went, the writ of the Pakistani state was more fragile than previously assumed.

American strategists faced a delicate balancing act. On one hand, the United States relied heavily on Pakistani cooperation for logistics, intelligence, and operations against al-Qaeda leadership. On the other, Washington questioned whether Islamabad possessed either the capacity or, in some quarters, the will to confront extremism decisively.

## The Broader Strategic Context

The Swat situation cannot be divorced from the larger regional dynamics. The porous border with Afghanistan facilitated the movement of fighters and materiel, complicating both the Afghan war effort and Pakistan's internal security. American drone strikes in the tribal regions, while tactically effective against certain targets, generated intense popular resentment and complicated the political position of Pakistan's civilian leadership.

Pakistan's military and intelligence services, meanwhile, maintained their own complex calculations regarding various militant factions—distinctions between groups deemed threats to the state and those historically viewed as strategic assets against India further muddied the picture.

The civilian government in Islamabad, still finding its footing after the return to democratic rule, confronted competing pressures: American demands for aggressive action, domestic war-weariness, and the genuine difficulty of imposing military solutions on complex insurgencies with local grievances.

## An Uncertain Future

Whether the Swat agreement would ultimately prove a durable peace or a hollow truce remained an open question fraught with implications. Should the militants honor their commitments and lay down arms, the deal might offer a template for addressing insurgency through political accommodation. Should they instead exploit the arrangement to entrench themselves and expand their influence, the agreement would stand as a cautionary tale about the limits of negotiation with committed extremists.

For the United States, the episode reinforced an uncomfortable reality: that counterterrorism success in the region depended ultimately on Pakistani will and capacity that Washington could influence but not control. The tools available to American policymakers—military aid, diplomatic pressure, intelligence cooperation, and targeted strikes—all carried limitations and unintended consequences.

The Swat Valley, once a symbol of Pakistan's natural beauty, had become instead a barometer of the nation's struggle to define itself and secure its future—a struggle whose outcome would reverberate far beyond its mountain valleys.

**WASHINGTON** — Senior U.S. and Pakistani officials met this week for high-stakes discussions on counterterrorism cooperation, as concerns mount over deteriorating security conditions in Pakistan's Swat Valley and the broader challenge of stabilizing neighboring Afghanistan.

The talks, which brought together diplomatic and defense officials from both nations, focused on coordinating efforts to combat militant networks operating along the volatile Afghanistan-Pakistan border region. Officials emphasized the need for a unified strategy as extremist groups continue to exploit ungoverned spaces in the region.

## A Deteriorating Situation in Swat

The discussions come against the backdrop of an increasingly precarious security environment in Pakistan's Swat Valley, once a popular tourist destination known for its scenic mountain landscapes. In recent months, the region has fallen under growing influence of militant factions, who have imposed harsh restrictions on the local population.

Reports from the area describe the destruction of schools—particularly those educating girls—along with attacks on security forces and the displacement of thousands of residents. The breakdown of governmental authority in Swat has raised alarm among both Pakistani and American officials, who view the region as a troubling indicator of the militants' expanding reach beyond the traditional tribal areas.

Pakistani authorities have struggled to reassert control, employing a combination of military operations and, at times, negotiated arrangements with militant leaders—approaches that have drawn scrutiny from Washington over their long-term effectiveness.

## Obama's Afghanistan Strategy

The bilateral talks also unfold as President Obama moves forward with plans to increase the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan. The decision to deploy additional troops reflects the administration's assessment that the security situation there requires reinforcement to counter a resurgent insurgency.

Administration officials have stressed that success in Afghanistan is closely tied to developments across the border in Pakistan, where militant safe havens continue to provide support and sanctuary to fighters crossing into Afghan territory. This interconnected view of the regional challenge—often described in policy circles as an "Af-Pak" strategy—has become central to the administration's approach.

The troop increase is intended to help stabilize contested areas, protect civilian populations, and buy time for the training of Afghan security forces capable of eventually taking the lead in their nation's defense.

## Balancing Cooperation and Sovereignty

A recurring theme in the discussions was the delicate balance between security cooperation and Pakistani sovereignty. Pakistani officials have expressed concerns about actions perceived as infringing on national territory, while U.S. representatives have underscored the urgency of denying militants their operational bases.

Both sides acknowledged that a durable solution requires not only military measures but also economic development, improved governance, and support for civilian institutions in the affected regions.

## Looking Ahead

As the talks concluded, officials from both nations signaled a commitment to continued engagement, even as significant challenges remain. The path forward will likely test the strength of the U.S.-Pakistan partnership, with the situations in Swat and Afghanistan serving as critical measures of success.

Analysts caution that the road ahead is fraught with difficulty, requiring sustained attention and cooperation to address the deeply rooted challenges facing the region. For both Washington and Islamabad, the stakes—regional stability and the containment of extremism—could hardly be higher.
